Build FIVE small, lightweight liquid-glass lower-third/tag motion graphics for a YouTube video edit, using HyperFrames. Budget mindset: these are simple single-element callouts (a short label + maybe an icon/accent), NOT full stat-card or title-reveal builds like the three that already exist in this project -- keep each one quick to build and reuse the same component/pattern across all five rather than re-deriving the design from scratch each time.

FIRST: read `C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Video Projects\tools\video-use\LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md` for the established palette/panel/motion recipe for this project -- use it directly, don't reinvent it. Then invoke the Skill tool with skill "hyperframes" for workflow guidance.

CONTEXT: Episode 1 of "Vibe Coding till I reach one paying customer" by creator Nick, building an app called Codely. Get exact word-level timestamps for each moment below from `C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Video Projects\first-video\edit\transcripts\screen.json` (top-level "words" array, `{"type":"word"|"spacing","text":...,"start":...,"end":...}`, seconds) -- don't estimate, read the real numbers.

BUILD A SHARED BASE COMPONENT FIRST: a small glass "tag" -- a compact pill/rounded-rect glass panel (frosted, backdrop-blur, subtle edge-highlight, soft shadow, liquid-glass palette from the style doc), sized to hold a short label (roughly 1-4 words) plus optionally a small icon/glyph. Design it once as a reusable pattern (parameterized by label text, accent color, and maybe icon), then instantiate it 5 times with different content/timing/duration below. Ease-out cubic entrance, ease-in cubic exit, never linear, never simultaneous multi-element reveals.

FIVE GRAPHICS TO BUILD (each its own composition dir + render, 1920x1080, 60fps, silent, WebM with VP9 alpha -- verify transparency by sampling actual pixel alpha values, e.g. via ffmpeg with `-c:v libvpx-vp9` explicitly, not by trusting a default ffprobe pix_fmt report which can be misleading per this project's LIQUID_GLASS_STYLE.md notes):

1. **"NEXION" tag** -- appears when he first names his earlier project. Find the word "Nexion" spoken near source ~172-180s (there are two mentions close together -- use the clearer/first one). Slot: `edit/animations/slot_tag_nexion/render.webm`. Small tag, bottom-left-ish or wherever won't conflict with a bottom-right webcam PIP, ~2-3s duration.

2. **"ROCKET.NEW" tag** -- appears when he names the comparison product. Find "Rocket.new" spoken near source ~247-259s. Slot: `edit/animations/slot_tag_rocket/render.webm`. Same style, ~2-3s.

3. **Bug-found callout** -- appears right when he identifies the bug. Find the moment around source ~708-718s ("Okay so obviously we have our first bug here"). Slot: `edit/animations/slot_tag_bug/render.webm`. Label something like "BUG FOUND" -- use a warning/attention accent tint (can lean slightly warmer/red within the established palette rather than the standard pink-peach-magenta, your call, but keep the glass-panel construction identical to the others), maybe a small warning-triangle or bug glyph. ~2s.

4. **Subscribe nudge** -- appears during the CTA. Find "hit that subscribe button" spoken near source ~365-390s (read the exact clean take's timestamps -- this line survives in the final cut around there). Slot: `edit/animations/slot_tag_subscribe/render.webm`. Label "SUBSCRIBE" with a little more energy/punch than the other tags (it's a call to action) but still liquid-glass, not a generic YouTube subscribe button graphic. ~2.5s, can have a subtle pulse/bounce on the icon if tasteful (ease-based, not linear).

5. **"NEW: AI Prompt Box" feature tag** -- appears when he explains the plan to add a prompt box. Find "I wanted to add a prompt box" spoken near source ~459-468s. Slot: `edit/animations/slot_tag_promptbox/render.webm`. ~2.5s.

PROCESS: build the shared component, verify it once (lint/check/snapshot, actually look at a frame), then produce the 5 instances efficiently. Verify each final render with ffprobe for duration/resolution, and confirm alpha transparency on at least the first one thoroughly (spot check corners = transparent on the rest, don't need to redo the full verification each time). Do not ask questions -- make sensible calls and proceed. Keep this efficient: reuse code/CSS across the five rather than rebuilding, and don't over-iterate on any single one.

Report back: for each of the 5, the render path, duration, and the exact source timestamp it's meant to start at in the final edit.

1	# Liquid Glass style reference
2	
3	Reusable design tokens for the "liquid glass" (iOS 26) motion-graphics style,
4	established across the Codely / Vibe Coding series. Reuse these values for
5	new graphics unless the video calls for a different brand explicitly.
6	
7	## Palette
8	
9	Warm pink → peach → magenta gradient (Codely's own brand gradient):
10	
11	```css
12	--glass-accent-1: #ff7aa8; /* pink */
13	--glass-accent-2: #ffb37a; /* peach */
14	--glass-accent-3: #ff6fae; /* magenta-pink */
15	--glass-accent-4: #cf3fc4; /* magenta */
16	/* typical usage: linear-gradient(135deg, var(--glass-accent-1), var(--glass-accent-2), var(--glass-accent-4)) */
17	```
18	
19	## Glass panel recipe
20	
21	- Backdrop blur + saturation boost on whatever sits behind the panel (`backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(1.4)`).
22	- Translucent fill, not solid: low-alpha white/brand-tinted background (~10-20% opacity), not a flat card color.
23	- Rounded corners, 20-32px radius depending on card size.
24	- Subtle white edge-highlight catching light at an angle (a `border` or inset gradient-masked ring, ~2-3px, ~40% opacity) -- this is the single most important cue that reads as "glass" rather than "flat card."
25	- Soft drop shadow, low opacity, generous blur -- glass should feel like it's floating, not pasted on.
26	- Optional: a one-shot diagonal sheen sweep on entrance (a light gradient streak animating across the panel) reads well for a reveal moment; skip it for anything that holds on screen a while, it gets busy.
27	
28	## Motion
29	
30	- Never linear easing. Ease-out cubic (`power2.out`/`power3.out`) for reveals landing on a payoff; ease-in cubic (`power2.in`) for exits.
31	- Never reveal two new elements simultaneously -- stagger, one beat at a time.
32	- Sync paydoffs to the actual spoken word/number, using real per-word timestamps from the transcript (`edit/transcripts/<source>.json`) -- never estimate timing from the phrase-level text alone.
33	
34	## Reusable code
35	
36	- `helpers/make_pip_assets.py` -- generates the rounded-mask/shadow/ring PNGs for a webcam PIP in this style.
37	- `helpers/composite_pip.py` -- composites webcam PIP / fullscreen / motion-graphic beats in this style; see its module docstring for the EDL schema.
38	- `helpers/zoom_filter.py` -- Ken-Burns push-in zoom, jitter-free (see its docstring for the ffmpeg gotchas it avoids -- worth reading before touching zoompan directly).
39	
40	## Alpha-transparent overlay graphics (HyperFrames → WebM)
41	
42	When a HyperFrames motion graphic is meant to overlay (not replace) existing
43	footage, render it to WebM with VP9 alpha and confirm transparency by actually
44	sampling pixel alpha values (corner should be `(0,0,0,0)`), not by trusting

HyperFrames **renders video from HTML** — a composition is an HTML file whose DOM declares timing with `data-*` attributes, whose animation runtime is seekable, and whose media playback is owned by the framework. | State                                                                                                                         | Action                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

| Explicit port of existing Remotion source to HyperFrames                                                                      | Read `references/routes/remotion-to-hyperframes.md`, then route directly to that workflow. Skip the intent layer.                                                                                           |
| Specific operation on an existing HyperFrames project: inspect, diagnose, validate, preview, render, publish, or batch-render | Perform only that operation. Skip intent and workflow routing; load `/hyperframes-cli` and any required domain skills.                                                                                      |
| Specific edit to an existing project                                                                                          | Make the edit. Do not run the intent layer.                                                                                                                                                                 |

Execute that workflow; `flow: companion` always executes in `/general-video`. Ask no brief questions.                                                                           |
| No brief, but `hyperframes.json` or `STORYBOARD.md` exists                                                                    | Resume from project files and recorded preferences. Infer the owning workflow from existing artifacts. If it cannot be determined uniquely, ask one routing-only question; do not run the intent interview. |
| Fresh creation                                                                                                                | Run the intent layer — `references/intent-interview.md` — then route once using § 2's table.                                                                                                                |

If a fresh request does not identify the subject or input, ask what the video is about before routing. Check preferences and recipes before asking anything (`references/intent-interview.md`, step 1). A `figma.com` input or a named recipe changes intake, not routing — the interview's "Adapt orthogonal inputs" section handles both.

### Keep the project's CLI current

A scaffolded project pins `hyperframes@<version>` in its `package.json` scripts so renders stay reproducible; the pin never advances on its own, and a pinned run of an older CLI prints no warning about it. When resuming a project whose scripts carry a pin, probe once before the first render-affecting command:

```bash
npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check
```

The probe is read-only and reports the pin against the latest release; keep the explicit `.` — on older CLI releases a bare `--project` followed by another flag consumes that flag as its directory value. When it reports the project behind — or any CLI output already shows it (the stderr notice `This project pins hyperframes@… (latest …)`, or `_meta.updateAvailable: true` in a `--json` result from a pinned script) — apply with `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .`, then verify with `npx hyperframes check`. A passing check confirms the project's compositions still validate on the new version — not that rendered output is frame-identical to the old pin — so a successful bump is never silent: name the old and new version in the run's summary. A project with no composition yet needs no verification. If the check fails, revert the `package.json` change, continue on the pinned version, and report which version the project stays on and why. Act on the signal rather than relaying it to the user; never leave a bumped pin unverified.

### Resolve common ambiguities

- A short animated title, logo sting, stat hit, chart hit, map hit, or standalone lower-third is `/motion-graphics` when it is unnarrated and motion is the message. A static title card, narrated sequence, longer montage, or custom loop is `/general-video`.
